newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma's Suu Kyi freed from house confinement - aide.
newsitem.headline: Burma's Suu Kyi freed from house confinement - aide.

text.p: Burma's pro-democracy opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi was released from confinement at her Rangoon home on Thursday and promptly called for her country to be excluded from the regional ASEAN bloc.

Suu Kyi, leader of the National League for Democracy (NLD), was permitted by the military State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) to attend a private wedding reception at a restaurant, two days after her confinement.

"It would be right to say that she has been released from confinement," an aide, who asked not to be named, told Reuters by telephone. Party leaders had earlier called her confinement "virtual house arrest".
SLORC officials were not immediately available for comment.
The Nobel laureate and daughter of independence hero Aung San later joined about 200 NLD members and supporters in a ceremony marking Burma's National Day at the home of an NLD leader.
Witnesses said police still blocked off roads leading to her house, the NLD headquarters and the site where the party ceremony took place in an apparent move to keep the foreign media away.
The SLORC restricted Suu Kyi to her home indefinitely on Tuesday in the wake of demonstrations by students of the Yangon Institute of Technology in Rangoon.
"It's essential and for the good of the country that...there must be understanding among all forces," Suu Kyi told reporters at the wedding reception.
"If we truly want law and order in this country, it has to be achieved through understanding, through a political settlement," she said.
SLORC has refused to hold a dialogue with the NLD, which won a landslide victory in the 1990 general election but was never allowed to govern.
Suu Kyi urged the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) not to grant Burma full membership as long as it is ruled by SLORC.
ASEAN said at the end of its summit in Jakarta on Saturday that it would simultaneously admit Burma, Laos and Cambodia as full members of the seven-member group, but did not say when.
"I think ASEAN countries are right to wait and see when it will be right for Burma to be a member of the organisation," Suu Kyi said.

"As I have already said, one day Burma should be a member of ASEAN because we do belong to the region," she said. "But for Burma under SLORC to be part of ASEAN, it will do the organisation no credit at all."

Diplomats said Suu Kyi's confinement reflected Rangoon's concern that she might be unknowingly drawn into the 20-hour campus and street demonstration by up to 2,000 students of the Yangon Institute of Technology early this week.
The protest, the biggest seen in the capital since the mass democracy uprisings in 1988, was triggered by anger at police handling of a brawl between students and restaurant owners in October.
Suu Kyi, who was released from six years' house arrest in July last year, said the roadblocks near the NLD headquarters were apparently meant to stop the party holding its meeting.
"This is no way to settle problems. You can't keep problems blocked up. They will just erupt in the end," she said.
